23–28 min. Compare two graphs with six nodes and five edges each. Left has an isolate and a bridge; right is a connected path. Ask who could receive a message if it travels only along observed ties. Equal size and density do not imply equal reachability.
The relational perspective
Attribute data describe actors: education, attitudes, resources.
Relational data describe ties: who contacts, trusts, or advises whom.
SNA asks how patterns of ties relate to social outcomes.
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1

28–32 min. A conventional table can store relational data too. The distinction is the substantive unit and dependence structure, not the file format. Mention that ties sharing actors may be dependent; independent-observation assumptions need care.

A graph is written G = (V, E): nodes V and edges E.

title: Weak ties and access to new information

text: Weak ties and access to new information
Close contacts often share overlapping social circles.
A tie between circles may provide access to different information.
A weak tie can serve this role, but not every weak tie is a bridge.
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1

40–45 min. Use C–D as a structural bridge in our undirected example. Tie strength has not yet been measured, so do not call it weak based on its position alone. Source: Granovetter (1973), The Strength of Weak Ties, https://doi.org/10.1086/225469. Avoid a universal claim that weak ties spread all information better.

title: The research question defines the network

text: The research question defines the network
Question: who seeks research advice from whom?
Nodes: all members of this research group.
Tie: person i names person j as a source of advice.
Time window: the previous four weeks.

45–49 min. This introduces the directed nomination version, not a claim that earlier undirected data encoded direction. Make clear that arrow direction must be stated.
Directed, undirected, and weighted ties
Directed: A names B as a source of advice.
Undirected: A and B co-authored a paper.
Weighted: A reports three advice interactions with B.
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1
49–53 min. Friendship survey nominations may be directed, even if everyday friendship is described as mutual. Weighted ties can represent frequency, intensity, duration, or distance; meanings differ.

text: 115–120 min. Convention: row=sender (seeker), column=receiver (advice source). A→B occupies row A, column B. Row sums are out-degree; column sums are in-degree.
Degree counts incident ties
Undirected degree: number of ties incident to a node.
Out-degree: number of outgoing ties.
In-degree: number of incoming ties.
The social meaning depends on what the tie records.
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1
120–124 min. All examples here are simple binary graphs without loops. Strength sums weights and is a different measure. An isolate has degree zero; low positive degree does not mean isolation.

title: Density is the fraction of possible ties

text: Density is the fraction of possible ties
Let n be the number of nodes and m the number of ties.
Undirected: possible ties = n(n − 1) / 2
Directed: possible ties = n(n − 1)
Density = observed ties / possible ties
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1
124–128 min. These formulas assume at most one edge per eligible pair, no self-loops, and n≥2. They are not formulas for summing interaction weights. Density is undefined by these formulas for n<2.
Activity: describe the six-person group

Undirected version: calculate each node’s degree.
Calculate the number of possible ties and the density.
For the directed version, find C’s in-degree and out-degree.
What changes if F is accidentally omitted?

title: What these measures can and cannot tell us

text: What these measures can and cannot tell us
Degree counts ties; it does not establish influence.
Equal density can coexist with different paths and components.
Density comparisons depend on network size and boundaries.

138–140 min. Return to the two networks at the start. Optional extension: mean degree = 2m/n = density × (n−1) for simple undirected networks. This is a relation between averages, not a claim about the full degree distribution.

title: One graph can have several layouts

text: One graph can have several layouts
Compare the fixed layout and a circular layout in the notebook.
Which properties stay the same?
Which visual impressions change?
Distance on the page is not automatically social distance.
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1
166–170 min. Four minutes. Layout changes do not change adjacency, degree, or density. The fixed arrangement was chosen for teaching and does not encode geography.
Classic results need careful interpretation
Short acquaintance chains were found among completed chains.
Hubs show unequal degree; a power law is a stronger claim.
A network pattern alone does not establish a causal process.
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1

170–173 min. Optional brief context rather than a new theory unit. Travers & Milgram (1969): 64 completed chains from 296 starters; mean 5.2 intermediaries in completed chains. This does not establish universal six-step reachability. https://snap.stanford.edu/class/cs224w-readings/travers69smallworld.pdf. Broido & Clauset (2019), Scale-free networks are rare: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-08746-5. Preferential attachment is one generative model, not established by a hub-shaped plot.
Exit question
A group has six actors and five undirected ties.
A colleague imports only the edge list and reports five actors.
What probably happened, and why does it affect density?
ADA III · Social Network Analysis · Session 1

173–177 min. Individual written response. Expected: an isolate may be missing; omitting it changes the denominator from 15 to 10 and raises density from .333 to .5. Five actors is consistent with the running example, but in a real dataset investigate rather than assume.
